newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan may seek tougher world tanker regulations.
newsitem.headline: Japan may seek tougher world tanker regulations.

text.p: Japan may propose more stringent international tanker regulations following a big oil spill last week in the Sea of Japan that fouled hundreds of km (miles) of Japanese coastline, government officials said on Thursday.

They added, however, that they were unlikely to copy the United States' approach of adopting unilateral measures to fight oil spills, arguing that the issue should be dealt with at the international level.

"It doesn't make much sense to work unilaterally for the safety of tanker operations as they (oil tankers) sail all around the world no matter which country they belong to," a transport ministry official said.
"Matters like this would better be left to the IMO (International Maritime Organisation)," he said. The IMO is a United Nations body dealing with maritime issues.

While ministry officials said they would not know what new measures to recommend until the cause of the accident was known, they cited stricter rules on tanker inspection and double-hulling of old tankers as possibilities.
Current IMO regulations require that all large tankers 25 years old or older be refitted with double hulls, which reduce the chance of an accidental spill.

The regulations, however, only apply to so-called dirty tankers, which carry crude and heavy oil, of 20,000 dead weight tonnes (dwt) or more, and so-called clean tankers, which carry lighter oil products such as gasoline, of 30,000 dwt or more.

The 26-year-old Russian-registered Nakhodka, which broke in two in the Sea of Japan on January 2 while carrying about 19,000 tonnes of grade C heavy fuel oil from China to Russia, was a 19,986-dwt dirty tanker. The spill was one of the worst in Japan's history.
Several oil industry sources suspected the Nakhodka was single-hulled, although an official at Japan's Maritime Safety Agency said this had not been confirmed.
Many shipowners are expected to resist stricter regulations on refitting with double hulls, industry sources said, as the massive cost usually forces the vessels to be scrapped altogether.

The transport ministry officials rejected suggestions that Japan might follow the lead of the United States, which adopted tough unilateral measures after the Exxon Valdez leaked 35,000 tonnes of crude oil into waters off the Alaskan coast.

The U.S. Oil Pollution Act of 1990, among other things, required tankers entering U.S. waters to carry documents guaranteeing that their owners can pay for cleanup operations and compensate fishermen or others who might suffer damage from a potential spill. -- Tokyo Energy Desk +81-3-3432-8837
